lines: Here are two answers to the same question.
Which one is better?
You pick one, it takes a second.
Now imagine that small choice made millions of times by thousands of people.
That is how today's AI assistants learn how to behave.
This is a story about the alignment problem.
Not a story about monsters, but about values, about who gets to decide them, and about how all of us can help.
The writer Alexander Solzhenitsyn observed that the line separating good and evil passes not between states or classes or political parties, but right through every human heart.
A language model learned from everything we have written, our kindness and our cruelty, our wisdom and our lies.
So that line runs through the model, too.
Alignment is the work of drawing it.
A language model begins by reading an enormous amount of text and learning to continue it.
That makes it capable.
It has seen kind answers and cruel ones, careful advice and dangerous advice, and it can continue any of them.
But it has no idea which of those we actually want.
Capable is not the same as aligned.
Alignment is the work of closing that gap, making a model helpful, honest, and harmless in the way people really mean.
The breakthrough was to stop writing rules for everything and to ask people instead.
A model writes two answers.
A person says which one is better.
That choice becomes data.
In reinforcement learning from human feedback, those choices train a reward model, a model of what people prefer.
The assistant is then trained to earn a high reward.
In 2022, people preferred the answers of a small model trained this way over a model 100 times larger without it.
A newer method, direct preference optimization, skips the reward model and learns from the pairs directly.
Either way, the model's behavior is shaped by our choices.
But preferences can pull a model in the wrong direction.
In April 2025, OpenAI rolled back an update to its model after it became overly flattering, praising and agreeing with users far too readily.
Their review found that a new reward signal based on thumbs up and thumbs down, together with other changes, had weakened what held flattery in check.
People tend to reward agreement.
The lesson is simple.
What we reward is what we get.
So, reward the answer that is honest and useful, not just the one that feels good.
So, where should the bar be?
Let's look at four questions where reasonable people can disagree.
Each one is a dial, and each one has to be set somewhere by someone for every model.
Question one, someone describes chest pressure and dizziness.
When should the model say, "See a doctor now?"
Too cautious, and it sends everyone to the doctor for everything and stops being useful.
Too confident, and it plays doctor itself.
OpenAI's guidelines say to give information without definitive advice that a licensed professional should give.
Anthropic's constitution describes a brilliant friend with a doctor's knowledge who gives real information and always points to emergency help when a life may be at risk.
Question two, what should a model keep private?
Your conversations, your health, your address, the names of the people you talk about.
A model that remembers you can help you more.
A model that remembers too much or shares it can hurt you.
In public deliberations run with Meta, people supported memory and personalization as long as users could see and control what is kept.
Question three, and the hardest, should a model ever report a user to the authorities?
Since 2025, OpenAI has said that when human reviewers find an imminent threat of serious harm to others, they may refer it to law enforcement, but not cases of self-harm to protect privacy.
In 2026, they broadened the criteria.
In simulated tests, an Anthropic model with tools told to act boldly sometimes emailed authorities about fraud it had been shown.
Anthropic described this as risky because the model may have incomplete or misleading information.
Trust and safety pull in different directions here.
There is no setting everyone agrees on, which is exactly why it should be decided in the open.
Question four, whose side is the model on?
You, the company that built it, or humanity as a whole?
OpenAI's model spec sets an order of authority.
Its own rules first, then the developers who build products, then the user.
Anthropic's constitution names three principles, Anthropic, operators, and users, but says it is not a strict hierarchy.
Some things users are entitled to cannot be overridden.
Good alignment lives in the overlap, helpful to you, honest with you, and safe for everyone else.
Which raises the deepest question of all, whose values?
In the Prism study, 1,500 people from 75 countries talked with 21 models and rated the answers.
Which model came out best depended on who was asked.
Researchers now talk about pluralistic alignment.
Models that can show a range of reasonable views that can be steered to your context, and that reflect the people they serve.
And there are early experiments in asking the public directly.
In 2023, about a thousand Americans helped write a constitution for a research model.
It shared about half its ideas with the company's own and put more weight on fairness and accessibility.
One hopeful trend is that values are being written down.
Constitutions and model specifications describe in plain language what a model should do and why.
Some are published openly and anyone can read them and argue with them.
Written values can be debated, compared, and improved.
Hidden values cannot.
And then, they can be measured with evaluations that test the same values in many languages so that a model that is aligned in English is also aligned in Swedish, Bulgarian, or Greek.
So, how can you take part?
More ways than you might think.
Vote.
In public arenas, people compare two anonymous answers and pick the better one.
Tens of millions of votes have shaped public leaderboards.
Rate honestly.
When you give a thumbs that is true and useful, not just the one that flatters you.
Join a deliberation.
Projects like the global dialogues ask a thousand people at a time across dozens of countries what they want from AI.
Build and review tests in your own language.
Volunteers once wrote over 160,000 messages in 35 languages for an open assistant.
Native speakers are still needed to review evaluations today.
And speak up when the rules are written.
Europe's code of practice for AI models drew input from over a thousand stakeholders.
The alignment problem is not a puzzle that a few engineers will solve once and for all.
It is an ongoing conversation about what we want from the most capable tools we have ever built.
Every vote, every rating, every test, and every argument moves the bar.
If that line runs through every human heart, then drawing it for our machines is a task for all of us.
Two answers on the table.
Which one would you choose?
